notes.meaning: Manasseh was the firstborn son of Joseph, and his family was given a special share of the promised land. His oldest son Machir was known as a mighty fighter, so his family had already settled the rugged grazing areas of Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan River. Now Joshua outlines the land given to the rest of the tribe on the west side of the river.

The remaining land west of the Jordan was divided among six other family clans descended from Manasseh. These groups included the families of Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher, and Shemida. Each clan received its own distinct territory to live in and cultivate.

A man named Zelophehad from the clan of Hepher died without leaving any sons. He left behind five daughters named Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. Under normal customs of the time, land only passed to sons, which meant this family line was in danger of losing its property.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some historical scholars view the account of Zelophehad's daughters as a later story written to explain why property laws were changed to allow women to inherit land.

notes.meaning: The five daughters boldly step forward before Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the tribal leaders to ask for their property. They remind the leaders that the Lord had specifically commanded Moses in the wilderness to give them an inheritance alongside their relatives. Joshua honors God's command and gives them their own share of the land.

Because of the daughters' claim, the land west of the Jordan was divided into ten distinct shares instead of six. Five shares went to the five male family clans, and five shares were divided equally among Zelophehad's five daughters. This division was in addition to the large regions of Gilead and Bashan already settled east of the Jordan.

The daughters of Manasseh received a full inheritance right alongside the male family lines of their tribe. Meanwhile, the eastern territory across the Jordan remained with the descendants of Machir. God showed that every family mattered to Him and was included in the blessings of His covenant promise.

The southern border of Manasseh ran from the town of Asher to Michmethath, near the city of Shechem. From there, the border line turned south toward the spring and settlement of En-tappuah. This line established the official boundary between Manasseh and their brother tribe, Ephraim.

The open countryside and farmlands of Tappuah belonged to the tribe of Manasseh, but the walled town itself belonged to Ephraim. This arrangement shows how closely connected the two brother tribes were as they shared the border region.

The boundary line continued south down to the Brook of Kanah and then traveled west all the way to the Mediterranean Sea. Several towns belonging to Ephraim were located inside Manasseh's territory north of the stream. Even with separate borders, the families of Joseph lived intermingled in peace.

Ephraim held the territory to the south, while Manasseh held the land to the north, bordered by the Mediterranean Sea to the west. On its northern side, Manasseh met the border of Asher, and on the east it bordered the tribe of Issachar. Together, these borders gave Manasseh one of the largest territories in the land of Canaan.

Manasseh was also given six important fortress towns located within the borders of Issachar and Asher, including Beth-shean, Endor, and Megiddo. These fortified cities guarded key valleys and trade routes across northern Canaan. They were valuable strategic locations for protecting the entire nation.

The people of Manasseh were not able to take control of these fortress towns right away because the Canaanites were firmly set on staying there. The Israelites lacked the courage and faith needed to drive out the enemy at that time. Giving in to fear kept them from enjoying the full inheritance God had provided.

Years later, when Israel grew stronger in population and military power, they still did not drive out the Canaanites completely. Instead, they forced them to pay tribute and do hard labor. They chose financial gain and compromise over complete obedience to God's command.

The tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh come together to complain to Joshua about their allotment. They argue that because the Lord had blessed them with such a huge population, they deserved more than just one combined lot. Perhaps because Joshua was from their tribe, they hoped he would give them special treatment.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some historical scholars think this complaint points to an older tradition in which the house of Joseph had only a single small allotment and held no land east of the Jordan.

notes.meaning: Joshua refuses to show favoritism to his own relatives and challenges them with their own words. He tells them that if they are truly such a great and numerous people, they should go up into the heavily forested hills of the Perizzites and Rephaites to clear land for themselves. True faith is shown by taking action rather than complaining.

The people of Joseph push back against Joshua's challenge. They object that the hill country is too small and difficult, while the fertile plains below are held by Canaanites equipped with terrifying iron chariots. Fear of the enemy's advanced weapons blinded them to God's greater power.

Joshua speaks directly to the house of Joseph and repeats his conviction with confidence. He tells them that because they are a large people with great strength, they indeed deserve more than just one cleared area. He encourages them to turn their complaint into action.

Joshua promises that the forested hill country will belong to them once they clear the timber. Even though the Canaanites in the plains have iron chariots and strong armies, God's people have the strength to drive them out. Trusting God allows His people to overcome obstacles that seem impossible.
